reason: The sources provide over 15 consistent, high-confidence claims across multiple major astronomical institutions regarding the 2019 dimming event and its mechanism.
story: In late 2019, the night sky changed. Betelgeuse, the massive red shoulder of Orion, suddenly lost over two-thirds of its brightness, plummeting from the 10th-brightest star to outside the top 20. Panic spread among astronomers and the public—was this the sign of an imminent supernova? The truth was even weirder. Betelgeuse didn't die; it 'burped.' A massive convection cell on the star's surface unleashed a titanic bubble of superhot plasma, moving at 200,000 miles per hour. This 'surface mass ejection' traveled millions of miles into space. As the gas cooled, it condensed into a colossal dust cloud that acted like a veil, masking the star from our perspective. By April 2020, the star returned to normal brightness, but the event left us with a terrifying realization: these stellar giants can undergo 'traumatic' outbursts that change their appearance in a matter of weeks.
angle: Betelgeuse suffered a 'traumatic' outburst, ejecting a massive plasma bubble that cooled into a giant dust cloud, effectively masking its own light.

claims.claim: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star located in the constellation of Orion.
In late 2019, Betelgeuse began to dim noticeably, losing more than two-thirds of its brilliance.
The dimming was so severe that the star dropped from the 11th-brightest to a record minimum by February 2020.
The dimming was caused by a massive cloud of dust blocking the star's light.
The dust cloud formed from superhot plasma ejected from the star's surface.
The plasma was unleashed by a massive convection cell on the star's surface.
The ejected material traveled at speeds of approximately 200,000 miles per hour.
The material cooled and formed dust grains once it reached millions of miles away from the star.
If Betelgeuse replaced our Sun, its surface would extend past the orbit of Jupiter.
Betelgeuse is approximately 10 million years old and is burning through its fuel rapidly.
Astronomers expect the star to explode as a supernova within the next 100,000 years.
When it goes supernova, the star will shine as bright as a half-Moon for over three months.
The supernova will be visible in the sky during the daytime for about a year.
Betelgeuse returned to its normal brightness range by April 2020.
The star is estimated to be roughly 700 to 725 light-years away from Earth.

disputed: The exact distance to Betelgeuse is disputed; estimates range from 400-600 light-years [S1] to 725 light-years [S2, S5]. A script should use 'roughly 700 light-years'.

Whether the dimming was caused solely by dust or a combination of dust and a cold starspot is debated; [S2] emphasizes dust while [S4] and [S7] suggest a hybrid model. A script should attribute the starspot theory to a 'hybrid model' or 'second team' of researchers.

The physical size of the star's surface varies in reports, ranging from extending past the asteroid belt [S1] to reaching Jupiter [S2, S6]. A script should use the Jupiter comparison as the more common visualization.
